title: Mathematical methods
scope: General-purpose mathematics a learner needs before or alongside the course, taught without reference to spacetime: single- and multivariable calculus (partial derivatives, chain rule, Taylor series, hyperbolic functions, Jacobians), abstract linear algebra (groups, vector spaces, bases, dual spaces, matrices, determinants, inverses, eigenvalues), Euclidean coordinates and parametrized curves and surfaces, three-dimensional vector calculus and its integral theorems, distributions (Dirac delta, Heaviside step), ordinary and partial differential equations with Green-function methods and the elliptic/hyperbolic distinction, Fourier analysis, perturbation methods, elementary Lie groups, and probability and statistics (noise models, Bayesian estimation, likelihood ratios). Point-set topology and maps for manifolds, curvature of curves and surfaces, index notation for spacetime tensors, and statistics applied to detector data are owned by their physics domains.

concepts.title: Identity versus equation
concepts.summary: An equation holds only for particular values of its unknowns, whereas an identity (often written with a triple bar) holds for every value because its terms cancel once expanded. Recognising which one is meant tells you whether a relation constrains anything.
concepts.notes: DIV uses the distinction when stating the Jacobi identity for Lie brackets; the same care matters later for the Bianchi identities, which hold for every metric.

concepts.title: Partial derivative
concepts.summary: The rate of change of a function of several variables with respect to one of them while all the others are held fixed. It is the basic building block of gradients, Jacobians and every field equation in the course.
concepts.notes: No dedicated book candidate: all three books assume it. Symmetry of mixed partial derivatives is the fact later used for integrability conditions and for torsion-free connections.

concepts.title: Chain rule
concepts.summary: The derivative of a composite function is the product of the derivatives of its parts; for several variables, a small change in the output is the sum over inputs of each partial derivative times that input's change. It is how coordinate differentials and derivative operators transform.
concepts.notes: Used constantly without comment in all three books (e.g. dx' = (dx'/dx) dx in GA ch02, df/dlambda along a path in GA ch03).

concepts.title: Taylor series
concepts.summary: A smooth function near a point is approximated by a polynomial whose coefficients are its derivatives at that point divided by factorials; truncating after a few terms gives controlled local approximations with big-O error estimates. The multivariable version expands in all coordinate displacements at once.
concepts.notes: Books use it silently for Newtonian limits, binomial expansions of gamma, Riemann normal coordinates and the Cauchy problem (DIV ch13 builds a wave-equation solution from its Taylor series; the printed series there omits 1/n!).

concepts.title: Hyperbolic functions
concepts.summary: cosh x and sinh x are the even and odd parts of the exponential, obeying cosh^2 x - sinh^2 x = 1 in the way cosine and sine obey a Pythagorean identity. They parametrise hyperbolas and are the natural language for rapidity, Lorentz boosts and uniformly accelerated motion.
concepts.notes: Books use them without teaching them (DIV ch03 rapidity, GA ch02 uniform acceleration, SCH ch11 Kruskal coordinates); the legacy curriculum-gap review flagged them as a needed bridge before rapidity and Rindler.

concepts.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus
concepts.summary: Integrating a derivative over an interval gives the difference of the function's values at the two ends, upper end counted positively and lower end negatively. Every later integral theorem (Green, Gauss, Stokes) has this same shape: a derivative inside, signed boundary values outside.

concepts.title: Abelian group
concepts.summary: A group is a set with an associative operation, an identity element and an inverse for every element; it is abelian when the operation is also commutative. Vector addition is the prototypical abelian group.
concepts.notes: SCH appendix A uses the term inside the vector-space axioms without defining it. Non-abelian examples met later: rotations, the Lorentz group.

concepts.title: Vector space
concepts.summary: A set whose elements can be added (forming an abelian group) and multiplied by real numbers, with the scalings distributing over sums and behaving associatively. Arrows, column vectors, matrices, functions and tangent vectors at a point are all examples.
concepts.notes: GA ch31 recalls the axioms to show tangent operators at a point form a vector space.

concepts.title: Linear independence
concepts.summary: A set of vectors is linearly independent when the only combination of them that gives the zero vector has all coefficients zero; otherwise some member can be written in terms of the others.

concepts.title: Basis and dimension
concepts.summary: The dimension of a vector space is the largest number of linearly independent vectors it contains, and a basis is any independent set of that size; every vector is then a unique combination of basis vectors, whose coefficients are its components.
concepts.notes: Abstract definition only; bases of spacetime vectors, dual bases and component transformation laws belong to tensor-algebra.

concepts.title: Dual vector space
concepts.summary: The set of all linear real-valued functions on a vector space is itself a vector space of the same dimension, called the dual; each basis of the original space induces a dual basis. Row vectors versus column vectors, and bras versus kets, are familiar instances.
concepts.notes: SCH ch03 names it once one-forms are seen to form a vector space; DIV ch05 identifies covectors at a point as the dual of the tangent space. The one-form machinery itself is in tensor-algebra.

concepts.title: Positive-definite inner product
concepts.summary: An inner product is positive definite when every nonzero vector has strictly positive square, A.A > 0; only then does it define a norm and ordinary lengths. The Minkowski metric is an inner product that fails this condition.
concepts.notes: Example folded in: the Frobenius inner product on n x n matrices (sum of products of corresponding entries, equal to the trace of A^T B), mentioned in SCH appendix A.

concepts.title: Matrix
concepts.summary: A rectangular array of numbers whose entry A_ij sits in row i and column j; square n x n matrices form a vector space of dimension n^2, and column vectors are n x 1 matrices.
concepts.notes: Folds in SCH appendix A naming conventions (dimension of a matrix, A_ij ordering, vector space of matrices) and GA appB underline-bold matrix notation.

concepts.title: Matrix multiplication
concepts.summary: The product AB has entries formed by pairing row i of A with column j of B and summing, (AB)_ij = sum_k A_ik B_kj; acting on a column vector is the special case. The product is associative but generally not commutative, and the identity matrix (Kronecker delta entries) leaves every matrix unchanged.

names: matrix action on a column vector
associativity and non-commutativity of matrix multiplication

merged_from: matrix action on a column vector
associativity and non-commutativity of matrix multiplication
concepts.notes: Square matrices with this product form an algebra (SCH appA). Reading index contractions as matrix products is covered in tensor-algebra.

concepts.title: Determinant
concepts.summary: A single number attached to a square matrix, ad - bc for 2 x 2 and in general computed by expanding along any row as entries times their cofactors (signed minors). It measures the signed volume scaling of the linear map and vanishes exactly when the matrix is not invertible.
concepts.notes: SCH appendix A defines it recursively via minors and cofactors. The alternating-symbol formula for determinants of tensors is in tensor-algebra; the signed-area picture is in differential-forms-and-frames.

concepts.title: Matrix inverse
concepts.summary: The inverse of a square matrix B is the matrix that multiplies B from either side to give the identity; it exists exactly when det B is nonzero, and its entries are the transposed cofactors divided by the determinant.

concepts.title: Orthogonal matrix
concepts.summary: A real matrix whose transpose is its inverse; such matrices are exactly the linear maps that preserve Euclidean lengths and angles, rotations being the standard example. Because they preserve the identity metric, vector and covector components transform the same way under them.
concepts.notes: GA ch01 uses the 2x2 rotation matrix as the warm-up for the Lorentz boost; SCH Ex 3.20 uses orthogonality to explain why Cartesian vector analysis never distinguishes vectors from one-forms.

concepts.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
concepts.summary: An eigenvector of a linear map is a nonzero vector that the map only rescales, and the scale factor is its eigenvalue; they are found from det(A - lambda I) = 0. Symmetric real matrices have real eigenvalues and an orthogonal set of eigenvectors, which diagonalises them.
concepts.notes: Named in the taxonomy but taught in no book as a topic; applied to the energy-momentum tensor (DIV ch12, owned by matter-and-stress-energy), principal curvatures (GA ch30) and tidal tensors.

concepts.title: Jacobi's formula
aliases: ln det M = Tr ln M
concepts.summary: The derivative of a determinant is the determinant times the trace of the inverse matrix times the derivative of the matrix, d(det A) = det A tr(A^{-1} dA); equivalently the variation of ln det A is tr(A^{-1} delta A). For the metric this gives the derivative of g used for the contracted Christoffel symbol and for varying sqrt(-g).
concepts.notes: DIV ch07 derives it by cofactor expansion; GA ch40 quotes the log-det form for the variation of the metric determinant.

concepts.title: Lie group
concepts.summary: A group whose elements depend smoothly on continuous parameters, so that group multiplication is a smooth operation; rotations, Lorentz boosts and gauge transformations are examples. Its infinitesimal elements form a Lie algebra.
concepts.notes: Only a biographical mention in GA ch33; specific groups (Lorentz, Poincare, isometry groups) belong to their physics domains.

concepts.title: Euclidean space
concepts.summary: The flat n-dimensional space of ordered n-tuples with distance given by Pythagoras, the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences; lengths, angles and all of Euclid's theorems follow. It is the model space that manifolds resemble locally.
concepts.notes: DIV ch02 uses Euclidean distance between simultaneous events as the Newtonian contrast to the spacetime interval.

concepts.title: Cartesian coordinates
concepts.summary: Coordinates that locate a point by signed distances along mutually perpendicular straight axes, so that the squared distance between nearby points is just the sum of squared coordinate differences.

concepts.title: Plane polar coordinates
concepts.summary: Coordinates (r, theta) on the plane giving distance from the origin and angle from an axis, with x = r cos theta and y = r sin theta. The line element becomes dr^2 + r^2 dtheta^2, the simplest example where coordinate components vary from place to place.
concepts.notes: GA ch03 uses it as the running example for every idea about coordinates; curvilinear bases and Christoffel symbols in polar coordinates belong to connection-and-parallel-transport.

concepts.title: Spherical polar coordinates
concepts.summary: Coordinates (r, theta, phi) on three-dimensional space built from a radius, a polar angle and an azimuth; the flat line element is dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, where dOmega^2 = dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2 is the line element of the unit sphere (the solid-angle element).
concepts.notes: The shorthand dOmega^2 (GA ch05) recurs in every spherically symmetric metric.

concepts.title: Conic sections
concepts.summary: The curves cut from a cone by a plane: circle, ellipse, parabola and hyperbola. With a focus at the origin they share the polar form 1/r proportional to 1 + e cos theta, with eccentricity e = 0, less than 1, equal to 1, or greater than 1.
concepts.notes: GA ch20 recovers them as the complete solution set of the Newtonian orbit equation; detailed ellipse geometry of orbits belongs to mechanics-and-newtonian-gravity.

concepts.title: Parametrized curve
concepts.summary: A curve described by coordinate functions x^mu(lambda) of a single parameter, so that points, tangent directions and rates of change along the path can be computed by differentiating with respect to lambda.
concepts.notes: DIV ch05 defines curves on a manifold the same way; tangent vectors built from curves belong to manifolds-and-metrics.

concepts.title: Parametrized surface
concepts.summary: A two- (or n-) dimensional region described by a map from parameters to points; the partial derivatives with respect to the parameters are tangent vectors, and small parameter steps span tiny parallelograms used to set up surface integrals.
concepts.notes: GA ch38 uses it to build the domain of integration in the generalized Stokes theorem.

concepts.title: Parametric versus implicit representation
concepts.summary: A curve, surface or subspace can be described either by giving its coordinates as functions of intrinsic parameters or by giving equations the coordinates must satisfy; for example the unit circle is (cos t, sin t) or x^2 + y^2 = 1. The number of parameters equals the dimension minus the number of independent constraints.

concepts.title: Jacobian determinant
concepts.summary: The determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of new coordinates with respect to old ones; it is the factor by which small coordinate volumes rescale, and where it is nonzero the change of coordinates is locally invertible (inverse function theorem).
concepts.notes: The inverse transformation has Jacobian 1/J (DIV ch05). GA ch38 shows the Jacobian emerging from wedge-product antisymmetry (owned by differential-forms-and-frames); the Jacobian matrix as transformation matrix belongs to manifolds-and-metrics.

concepts.title: Gradient
concepts.summary: For a scalar function in Euclidean space, the vector of its partial derivatives; it points in the direction of fastest increase, has magnitude equal to that rate, and is perpendicular to surfaces of constant value.
concepts.notes: Reinterpreting the gradient as a one-form rather than a vector is taught in tensor-algebra.

concepts.title: Directional derivative
concepts.summary: The rate of change of a function along a given vector v, equal to v . grad f = v^i df/dx^i; heuristically the value at the tip of a small v minus the value at its base. It is the template that covariant derivatives and tangent-vector operators generalise.
concepts.notes: GA ch31 reinterprets it as the action of a tangent vector on a function and as the pairing of v with df; those readings are developed in manifolds-and-metrics and differential-forms-and-frames.

concepts.title: Lagrange multiplier
concepts.summary: To extremise a function subject to a constraint, extremise the function minus an unknown multiplier times the constraint; at the solution the two gradients are parallel, and the multiplier measures how the optimum shifts as the constraint is relaxed.
concepts.notes: GA ch30 uses it for extreme normal curvatures, where the multiplier turns out to be an eigenvalue.

concepts.title: Divergence
concepts.summary: For a vector field, the sum of the derivatives of each component along its own direction, div A = dA_x/dx + dA_y/dy + dA_z/dz; it measures net outflow per unit volume from a tiny box around a point.
concepts.notes: No book teaches it as a topic; the covariant divergence and its polar-coordinate form belong to connection-and-parallel-transport.

concepts.title: Curl
concepts.summary: For a vector field in three dimensions, the vector whose components measure the circulation per unit area around small loops in each coordinate plane; it vanishes for gradient fields.
concepts.notes: Needed for the Kelvin-Stokes theorem; its identification as the Hodge dual of an exterior derivative is in differential-forms-and-frames.

concepts.title: Laplacian
concepts.summary: The divergence of the gradient, which in Cartesian coordinates is the sum of unmixed second partial derivatives; in plane polar coordinates it reads (1/r) d/dr (r dphi/dr) + (1/r^2) d^2phi/dtheta^2, the same operator in different coordinates.
concepts.notes: SCH ch05 derives the polar form by raising the gradient one-form to a vector and applying the covariant divergence, showing a memorised formula follows from tensor calculus.

concepts.title: Divergence theorem
concepts.summary: The outward flux of a vector field through a closed surface equals the volume integral of its divergence over the enclosed region. It turns global conservation or flux laws, such as Gauss's law, into local differential equations and back.
concepts.notes: Folds in the volume gradient theorem (GA ch38): the integral of a gradient over a volume equals the boundary integral of the function times the outward surface element, from which the divergence theorem follows componentwise. The curved-space and tensor-density versions belong to manifolds-and-metrics; the generalized Stokes theorem to differential-forms-and-frames.

concepts.title: Green's theorem in the plane
concepts.summary: For a region of the plane bounded by an anticlockwise closed curve, the circulation of L dx + M dy around the curve equals the area integral of dM/dx - dL/dy over the region.

concepts.title: Kelvin-Stokes theorem
concepts.summary: The flux of the curl of a vector field through an oriented surface equals the circulation of the field around the surface's boundary curve, with the direction of travel fixed by the right-hand rule.
concepts.notes: GA ch38 derives it from a surface identity with the Levi-Civita symbol and then as a case of the generalized Stokes theorem.

concepts.title: Dirac delta function
concepts.summary: A distribution concentrated at a single point with unit total integral, defined by its sifting action: integrating it against a smooth function returns that function's value at the point. Higher-dimensional deltas are products of one-dimensional ones and represent point sources.
concepts.notes: Not a genuine function (DIV ch22 warns). Example folded in: the four-dimensional delta (GA ch12), which divided by sqrt(-g) becomes a scalar; its use for point-particle world lines belongs to matter-and-stress-energy.

concepts.title: Heaviside step function
concepts.summary: The function that is 0 for negative argument and 1 for positive argument; its derivative in the distributional sense is the Dirac delta.
concepts.notes: DIV ch22 introduces it with the identities theta' = delta and u delta(u) = 0 before building impulsive gravitational waves.

concepts.title: Laplacian of 1/r
concepts.summary: The Laplacian of 1/|x - x'| vanishes everywhere except at x = x', where it equals -4 pi times a three-dimensional delta function; equivalently the inverse-square field of a point has divergence 4 pi delta. This single identity links point masses and charges to Poisson's equation.
concepts.notes: GA ch13 quotes it to convert the integral form of Newtonian gravity into a differential law, with proof via Gauss's theorem left as an exercise.

concepts.title: Ordinary differential equation
aliases: initial value problem for an ODE
concepts.summary: An equation relating an unknown function of one variable to its derivatives; a linear equation of order n needs n pieces of initial data (such as position and velocity) to fix a unique solution, and any such equation can be rewritten as a first-order system.
concepts.notes: Assumed by all books (orbit equations, Friedmann equation, TOV equation); the legacy course teaches it as a bridge, with exponential decay and the harmonic oscillator as examples.

concepts.title: Laplace's equation
concepts.summary: The equation nabla^2 f = 0; its solutions in a source-free region are smooth, and one that vanishes at infinity outside a bounded region falls off as a constant over r plus faster-decaying multipole terms.

names: multipole falloff of solutions of Laplace's equation

merged_from: multipole falloff of solutions of Laplace's equation
concepts.notes: DIV ch04 obtains it as the vacuum case of Poisson's equation (which as the law of gravity belongs to mechanics-and-newtonian-gravity); SCH ch08 uses the multipole falloff to read off the mass from the far field.

concepts.title: Green's function
aliases: Green's function solution of Poisson's equation
concepts.summary: For a linear differential operator L, the Green's function G is its response to a point source, L G = delta; the solution for any source is then the superposition of G over the source. For Poisson's equation this gives the familiar integral of the source divided by distance, with a 1/(4 pi).

names: Green's function solution of Poisson's equation

merged_from: Green's function solution of Poisson's equation
concepts.notes: Worked instance folded in: the static Green's function -1/(4 pi |x - x'|) of the Laplacian (GA ch13, ch42, ch47).

concepts.title: Wave equation
concepts.summary: The second-order partial differential equation stating that the second time derivative of a field equals the wave speed squared times its Laplacian (the d'Alembertian of the field vanishes); its solutions are non-dispersive disturbances moving at that speed, built from plane waves.
concepts.notes: Arises in GA ch14 as the matter-free field equation, in GA ch40 from a string Lagrangian, and in DIV ch13 as the toy model for the Cauchy problem. The d'Alembertian operator itself is in tensor-algebra; its gravitational-wave instances belong to gravitational-waves.

concepts.title: Fourier transform
concepts.summary: Rewriting a function of time or space as a superposition of complex exponentials, one amplitude per frequency or wavenumber; derivatives become multiplications, which turns linear constant-coefficient equations into algebra and makes noise spectra and correlations easy to compute. Sampled data use the discrete version, computed quickly by the FFT.
concepts.notes: No book teaches it as a topic; SCH Ex 12.4 uses it to explain the efficiency of frequency-domain template searches (the printed Eq. 12.41 has a stray factor).

concepts.title: Retarded Green's function
aliases: fundamental solution of the wave equation
concepts.summary: The causal solution of the wave equation for a point source that flashes once: a spherical shell expanding at the wave speed with amplitude falling as 1/r, delta(t - r)/(4 pi r). Superposing it over a source gives retarded potentials evaluated at the time the signal left each source point.

names: fundamental solution of the wave equation

merged_from: fundamental solution of the wave equation
concepts.notes: DIV ch21 builds it from a spherically symmetric point source before solving the linearized Einstein equations; the radiation applications belong to gravitational-waves.

concepts.title: Hyperbolic partial differential equation
concepts.summary: A partial differential equation whose highest-derivative terms have the structure of a wave operator, so that disturbances propagate at finite speed along characteristics and the Cauchy problem (data on an initial surface) is well posed. Elliptic equations like Laplace's behave very differently: their solutions are fixed by boundary data and respond instantly everywhere.
concepts.notes: DIV ch13 invokes it to explain why the reduced Einstein equations can use standard PDE theory. Cauchy-Kovalevskaya and well-posedness of the Einstein equations belong to einstein-field-equations.

concepts.title: Analytic function
concepts.summary: A function equal to its convergent Taylor series near every point; its value and all derivatives at one point then fix it throughout a connected domain, which is far more rigid than mere smoothness.
concepts.notes: DIV ch13 assumes analytic data to rebuild the metric from time derivatives and then points out that analyticity conflicts with causality, since a smooth bump of compact support is not analytic.

concepts.title: Perturbation theory
concepts.summary: When an equation contains a small dimensionless parameter epsilon, write the solution as a zeroth-order solution plus epsilon times a correction plus higher orders, and solve order by order; nondimensionalising first makes clear which terms are genuinely small.
concepts.notes: DIV ch16 applies it in parallel to perihelion precession and light bending. Linearized gravity and second-order gravitational-wave perturbation theory belong to gravitational-waves.

concepts.title: Secular term
concepts.summary: A term in a perturbative solution that grows without bound with the independent variable, like phi sin phi, produced by forcing at the system's own natural frequency; it signals a slow cumulative change such as a shifted frequency, and resumming it restores a bounded solution.
concepts.notes: DIV ch16 identifies the secular term as the source of perihelion advance and resums it into cos[phi(1 - epsilon)].

concepts.title: Linear stability analysis
concepts.summary: Write a quantity as an equilibrium value plus a small deviation, keep only first-order terms in the equations of motion, and check whether the deviation oscillates (stable) or grows (unstable).
concepts.notes: GA ch18 applies it to show the Einstein static universe is unstable.

concepts.title: White noise
concepts.summary: Random noise whose values at different times are statistically uncorrelated, so the covariance of samples is a variance times a Kronecker delta and its power spectrum is flat across frequencies.
concepts.notes: SCH ch12 adopts it as a simplifying assumption to expose matched filtering, noting real detector noise is coloured. Detector noise and matched filtering belong to gravitational-wave-astronomy.

concepts.title: Bayesian parameter estimation
concepts.summary: Combine the likelihood of the observed data given model parameters with prior probabilities to obtain a posterior probability distribution over the parameters, which yields best estimates and credible intervals.
concepts.notes: SCH ch12 shows its output for gravitational-wave measurements of H0 and contrasts it with frequentist significance; the detection pipeline itself belongs to gravitational-wave-astronomy.

concepts.title: Likelihood ratio
concepts.summary: The ratio of the probability of the data under one hypothesis to that under another, for example signal plus noise versus noise alone; thresholding it gives the optimal detection statistic, and the ratio of marginal likelihoods (the Bayes factor) compares models.
concepts.notes: Named in the taxonomy as mathematical-methods; SCH ch12 quotes Bayes factors for the GW170814 polarization test, which belongs to gravitational-wave-astronomy.

concepts.title: Gaussian noise
concepts.summary: Random noise whose samples (or frequency-bin amplitudes) follow a zero-mean normal distribution with a variance that does not change in time. It is the default model for detector noise because many small independent disturbances add up to a normal distribution, and it makes false-alarm rates computable from the Gaussian tail.
concepts.notes: Contrast with non-Gaussian glitches in real detector data.
